faq.q: Can I give a peripheral nerve block to a patient on anticoagulants?

faq.a: It reduces systemic absorption, prolongs block duration, and provides a visual cue of intravascular injection (bright red blood).

exam: A 25‑year‑old with a tibial fracture needs surgery but has severe asthma – which anaesthetic technique would you choose and why? — Choose a femoral and sciatic nerve block to avoid airway manipulation and reduce opioid need.
During a brachial plexus block the patient develops a seizure – what is your immediate management? — Stop injection, call for help, secure airway, give 20 % lipid emulsion, monitor cardiac rhythm.

Explain how you would confirm correct needle placement for a popliteal sciatic block without ultrasound. — Use a nerve stimulator, look for foot dorsiflexion/plantarflexion at <0.5 mA, aspirate before injection.
A patient on warfarin (INR 3.0) requires an ankle block – what do you do? — Correct INR to ≤1.5 or choose an alternative analgesic; deep blocks are contraindicated with high INR.

What are the key differences between a femoral nerve block and a fascia‑iliaca compartment block? — Femoral block targets the nerve directly under the fascia lata; fascia‑iliaca spreads local anaesthetic under the fascia to reach the femoral nerve indirectly, useful when landmarks are difficult.
List three early signs of compartment syndrome after a lower‑limb block and the next step. — Pain out of proportion, tense swelling, paresthesia; obtain urgent surgical consultation for fasciotomy.

Why might a patient with diabetic peripheral neuropathy have a false‑negative sensory test after a block? — Baseline loss of sensation can mask block effect; rely on motor testing and patient‑reported change.
Describe the contraindications to performing a supraclavicular brachial plexus block. — Infection at site, coagulopathy, severe lung disease (risk of pneumothorax), patient refusal.
ai.title: Peripheral Nerve Blocks
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Peripheral nerve blocks are targeted injections of local anaesthetic that temporarily interrupt nerve conduction for surgery or pain relief. Understanding anatomy, technique, indications, and complications lets clinicians use them safely, especially where resources are limited.

b: Provides site‑specific analgesia
Reduces systemic opioid side‑effects
Useful in patients with respiratory disease or limited monitoring
sections.p: A peripheral nerve block (PNB) involves injecting local anaesthetic near a named peripheral nerve or plexus to produce a reversible loss of sensation and motor function in its distribution. It can replace or supplement general anaesthesia, reduce opioid needs, and improve postoperative recovery.

b: Identify the nerve/plexus (e.g., femoral, sciatic, brachial plexus)
Use a nerve stimulator (motor twitch at <0.5 mA) or ultrasound to confirm proximity
Select a long‑acting agent (e.g., bupivacaine) for surgery, shorter‑acting (e.g., lidocaine) for diagnostic blocks
sections.p: Success depends on three pillars: (1) precise knowledge of nerve anatomy and surface landmarks, (2) correct needle placement (often guided by nerve stimulator or ultrasound), and (3) appropriate choice of local anaesthetic and adjuvant.

b: Upper‑limb surgery – brachial plexus or individual nerve blocks
Lower‑limb fracture fixation – femoral, sciatic, or ankle blocks
Cesarean section – combined spinal‑epidural with pudendal block for postoperative pain
sections.p: In low‑resource hospitals, PNBs can enable surgery without a ventilator, limit opioid consumption, and allow early mobilisation, which is crucial for trauma, orthopaedic, and obstetric cases.

b: Know the sensory and motor territories of each block
List absolute contraindications (infection at site, patient refusal, coagulopathy)
Describe early signs of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (CNS agitation, seizures, cardiac arrhythmia)
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to choose, perform, and manage complications of PNBs. Focus on anatomy, indications, contraindications, and recognition of toxicity.

b: Assuming surface landmarks are sufficient without nerve stimulator/ultrasound
Injecting large volumes into a confined compartment (risk of compartment syndrome)
Neglecting to aspirate before injection, increasing intravascular injection risk
sections.p: Errors often arise from incomplete anatomical knowledge, inadequate needle positioning, or failure to monitor for toxicity.

t.b: Can it be used to visualise nerve and needle? – If yes, improves success and reduces complications; if not, rely on nerve stimulator and landmarks.
Is the patient coagulopathic? – Normal results allow block; abnormal results require correction or alternative analgesia.
Any cardiac conduction abnormality? – Important before using agents that may cause arrhythmias in toxicity.

b: Local anaesthetic: choose bupivacaine for long surgery, lidocaine for short diagnostic block
Adjuvant: add epinephrine (1:200 000) to prolong block and reduce systemic absorption
If toxicity occurs: stop injection, call for help, secure airway, give 20 % lipid emulsion bolus
sections.p: Perform the block, monitor, and treat complications promptly. Always have resuscitation equipment and lipid emulsion ready for systemic toxicity.

b: Spinal anaesthesia – injects into CSF, produces bilateral lower‑body block
Epidural – catheter placed in epidural space for continuous infusion
Field block – infiltrates tissue around incision, not targeting a specific nerve
sections.p: Distinguish peripheral nerve blocks from spinal/epidural anaesthesia and from field blocks (e.g., local infiltration).

b: Rely on patient report of loss of pin‑prick sensation, not just motor response
In patients with peripheral neuropathy, sensory testing may be unreliable
sections.p: A successful motor twitch does not guarantee adequate sensory block; conversely, lack of twitch may be due to deep nerve location rather than failure.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (seizure, arrhythmia, loss of consciousness)
Rapidly expanding limb swelling suggesting compartment syndrome
Persistent severe pain despite block indicating possible intraneural injection
